agentInstructions.text: Use Home Assistant to look things up before writing anything. Never guess an entity ID: find it with list_entities (filter by domain and search) and read its attributes with get_state. Confirm a service and its fields with list_services before calling it, and check a Jinja condition or value_template with render_template against live state before you put it in YAML. Use get_history, get_logbook, get_error_log and check_config to diagnose an automation that did not fire. Author automations, scripts and scenes in the Home Assistant configuration repository and deploy them the normal way: this connection deliberately has no tool that writes automations.yaml, because rewriting that file through the API conflicts with a Git-managed configuration. call_service acts on the real house and can switch devices, unlock locks or reload configuration, so target the narrowest entity that does the job, prefer a reversible action, and do not call it to explore. Respect action permissions and approvals; if a call fails, report what did and did not happen rather than retrying a service call that may already have taken effect.

name: Home Assistant
description: Look up entities and live state in Home Assistant and call its services.

methods.label: Long-lived access token
methods.whenToUse: Use a long-lived access token to read entities and live state and to call services on your own Home Assistant instance.

tenantFields.label: Home Assistant address
tenantFields.helperMd: The address you open Home Assistant at, without a trailing `/api`. A private or LAN address works when this Paperclip deployment is not publicly exposed.

credentialFields.label: Long-lived access token
credentialFields.helperMd: A Home Assistant long-lived access token inherits every permission of the account that created it. Home Assistant does not support scoping a token to specific entities, domains or read-only use, so the credential field tells the operator to issue the token from an account carrying only the access its agents need, and the connector's write surface is a single destructive action (home_assistant_call_service), and the two read actions that can return a credential in provider text (home_assistant_get_error_log, home_assistant_check_config) are classified write, so all three default to Ask first and an operator can set any of them to Off. Paperclip cannot reduce an already-issued token's permissions; revoking it in the Home Assistant profile screen is the immediate cut-off.

methods.guidanceMd: In Home Assistant open your profile → **Security** → **Long-lived access tokens** → **Create token**, then paste it below with your instance address. The token inherits your own Home Assistant permissions, so create it from an account with only the access your agents need.
warnings: A long-lived access token carries the full permissions of the Home Assistant account that created it. Home Assistant cannot narrow it to specific entities or domains.

home_assistant_get_error_log and home_assistant_check_config return raw provider text. An integration logs the URL of a failed request, and a YAML validation error quotes the offending value with any !secret already expanded, so either can contain a token or password. Both ship Ask first; review the action policy before setting either to Allowed.
Calling a service acts on real devices. Review the action policy for home_assistant_call_service before leaving it Allowed.
This connector does not write automations.yaml. Authoring automations through the API rewrites that file in place, which conflicts with a Git-managed configuration.
